triage.name: Angina
triage.reason: Chest pain is a classic undifferentiated symptom case; history, ECG, and troponin lead to stable angina versus ACS and its mimics.

rule_errors: workup.initial: unknown test id 'ecg'; use a listed id or the test's plain name
workup: 'chest x-ray' appears in ['initial', 'supporting', 'not_indicated']; use one group, or not_indicated plus one entry with only_if

demographics: More common in men than women before age 60; the gap narrows after menopause
More common in Black adults and in South Asian adults in the US, largely tracking higher rates of hypertension and diabetes
Often first noticed when a person becomes less active or gains weight

risk_factors.text: Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
Cigarette smoking or long-term secondhand smoke exposure
Age over 55 in men or over 65 in women
Family history of early heart disease

family_history: Heart attack or coronary bypass in a father or brother before age 55
Heart attack or coronary bypass in a mother or sister before age 65
Sudden cardiac death in a close relative
social_history: Lives in a neighborhood with limited access to fresh food or safe walking areas

chief_complaints.text: My chest feels tight and heavy when I walk up the stairs
It feels like someone is standing on my chest
I get a pressure in my chest that goes away when I sit down
My chest hurts and the pain runs down my left arm
It feels like bad indigestion when I exert myself

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months; the pattern becomes predictable
hpi.duration: Each episode lasts about 2 to 10 minutes and resolves within minutes of stopping the activity
hpi.progression: Started with heavy exertion only, then began coming on with lighter activity such as one flight of stairs or walking uphill; frequency and ease of triggering have slowly increased
hpi.location: Mid-chest, behind the breastbone; may be described as the whole front of the chest
hpi.radiation: Often to the left shoulder and inner left arm; sometimes to the neck, jaw, back, or upper abdomen
hpi.quality: Pressure, squeezing, tightness, heaviness, or a band-like ache; rarely sharp or stabbing
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, usually 3–6/10; the patient often stops what they are doing rather than calling it severe pain
hpi.timing: Comes on during exertion or emotional stress and eases within a few minutes of rest; reproducible with the same level of activity
relieving: Nitroglycerin under the tongue within 1–5 minutes

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath with the chest discomfort
Feeling of doom or anxiety during the episode
Fatigue with activity that used to be easy

pertinent_negatives: Pain that is sharp and worse with a deep breath or lying flat
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain that lasts only seconds or is constant for hours
Pain that is burning and worse after meals or when lying down
Recent long car or plane trip with one-sided leg swelling
Sudden tearing pain that moves from the chest to the back
Pain that comes only with eating or is relieved by antacids

negatives: Chest pain at rest lasting more than 20 minutes
Pain that wakes them from sleep
argues_against: Pain at rest that is not relieved by nitroglycerin

positives.text: Short of breath when the chest discomfort comes on

negatives: Pleuritic pain worse with deep breath

positives.text: Belching that the patient blames on heartburn

negatives: Pain that is clearly worse after meals or when lying down
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain worse with twisting or reaching
argues_against: Pain only with certain arm movements

positives.text: Worry that something is wrong with the heart

negatives: Panic attacks that come at rest without exertion
Symptoms that only occur during stressful situations with no exertional trigger
argues_against: Chest pain only during panic attacks

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with shortness of breath, weakness, or confusion rather than chest pain; episodes can be triggered by minimal activity.
Neuropathy from long-standing diabetes can blunt the pain, so they report breathlessness, fatigue, or indigestion instead of classic chest pressure.
Chest discomfort is more often attributed to reflux or the increased workload of pregnancy; true angina is uncommon but can occur with pre-existing coronary disease or coronary spasm.
Symptoms come on with much lighter activity, and shortness of breath may dominate over chest pressure.
missing_classic_features: Chest pain as the main complaint

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress at rest; normal appearance
general.moderate: Mild anxiety or discomfort during episodes, otherwise comfortable at rest
general.severe: Diaphoretic, anxious, appears uncomfortable even at rest
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, distressed, may be hypotensive or in pulmonary edema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the chest wall and reproduce symptoms by pressing on the sternum and ribs
findings.finding: No chest wall tenderness

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex, base, and Erb's point
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops

findings.maneuver: Auscultate at the apex with the bell
findings.finding: S3 gallop suggesting left ventricular dysfunction or volume overload

findings.maneuver: Auscultate at the apex with the bell
findings.finding: S4 gallop suggesting reduced left ventricular compliance
Carotid bruits suggesting concomitant atherosclerotic disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the jugular venous pulse at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure suggesting heart failure or right heart strain
Bibasilar crackles suggesting pulmonary congestion

findings.maneuver: Press the dorsum of each foot and the lower legs
findings.finding: Pitting edema suggesting right heart failure

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses
findings.finding: Diminished or absent peripheral pulses suggesting diffuse atherosclerosis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelids, tendons, and skin for lipid deposits
findings.finding: Xanthelasma or tendon xanthomas suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia

findings.maneuver: Palpate the Achilles tendons and extensor tendons of the hands
findings.finding: Tendon xanthomas suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea for a gray-white ring at the limbus
findings.finding: Arcus senilis suggesting hyperlipidemia

labs.caveat: Normal or essentially unchanged serial troponins separate stable angina from unstable angina and myocardial infarction; a rise or fall indicates acute myocardial injury.
Anemia lowers oxygen delivery and can worsen or unmask angina; also relevant before considering antianginal therapy.
Diabetes is a major risk factor and complicates management; hyperglycemia can worsen ischemia.
Baseline kidney function guides medication dosing and contrast exposure.
Elevated LDL supports atherosclerotic risk and determines lipid-lowering therapy.
Low HDL is a risk marker but not a treatment target.
Identifies undiagnosed diabetes or poor control, both of which worsen prognosis.
Elevated BNP suggests heart failure as an alternative or contributing cause of dyspnea and chest discomfort.
Thyroid disease can precipitate or mimic angina; consider when symptoms are atypical or there are thyroid features.

findings.finding: Sinus rhythm
Horizontal or downsloping ST depression during pain or with exercise
T wave inversion in the ischemic territory
Transient ST elevation during spontaneous rest pain (coronary vasospasm)
Pathologic Q waves from prior myocardial infarction
Left bundle branch block or other intraventricular conduction delay
Left ventricular hypertrophy from long-standing hypertension
Prolonged QT interval

findings.text: Normal left ventricular systolic function
Regional wall motion abnormality in a coronary distribution
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Diastolic dysfunction
Valvular disease such as aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation

imaging.study: Exercise or pharmacologic stress test with imaging (nuclear perfusion or echocardiography)
imaging.preferred_when: Patients who can exercise and have interpretable ECG; pharmacologic stress if unable to exercise

findings.text: Reversible perfusion defect in a coronary territory during stress
Fixed perfusion defect suggesting prior infarction
New or worsening regional wall motion abnormality with stress
Normal perfusion and function (negative study)

imaging.preferred_when: Lower-risk patients with atypical symptoms and no known coronary disease

findings.text: Coronary artery calcification and atherosclerotic plaque
Stenosis of one or more coronary arteries
No significant coronary stenosis (negative study)

imaging.preferred_when: High-risk features, refractory symptoms, or when revascularization is being considered

findings.text: Significant stenosis in one or more epicardial coronary arteries
Multivessel coronary artery disease
Left main or proximal left anterior descending stenosis
No obstructive disease (possible vasospastic or microvascular angina)
Normal heart size and clear lungs
Cardiomegaly suggesting heart failure
Pulmonary venous congestion or edema
Widened mediastinum suggesting aortic dissection

initial.why: First test in any chest pain; identifies ischemia, infarction, or arrhythmia
Distinguishes stable angina from unstable angina or myocardial infarction; serial measurements if initially normal
Detects anemia that can worsen ischemia
Baseline kidney function, electrolytes, and glucose before therapy
Assesses atherosclerotic risk and guides lipid-lowering therapy
Screens for diabetes, a major modifiable risk factor
Evaluates alternative causes of chest pain and heart size
initial.only_if: another cause of chest pain is suspected or the presentation is atypical

initial.why: Assesses ventricular function and valvular disease
initial.only_if: heart failure, murmur, or prior infarction is suspected

confirmatory.test: Exercise or pharmacologic stress test with imaging (nuclear perfusion or echocardiography)
confirmatory.why: Confirms inducible ischemia and risk-stratifies when the diagnosis is uncertain and the patient is stable
Noninvasive anatomic confirmation in lower-risk patients with atypical symptoms
Definitive anatomic diagnosis and allows revascularization when high-risk features or refractory symptoms are present

supporting.why: Thyroid disease can precipitate or mimic angina
supporting.only_if: atypical features or suspected thyroid disorder

supporting.why: Helps identify heart failure as an alternative or contributing cause
supporting.only_if: dyspnea predominates or heart failure is suspected

supporting.why: Rules out pulmonary embolism when the presentation is atypical
Evaluates alternative causes of chest pain
supporting.only_if: another cause of chest pain is suspected or the presentation is atypical

not_indicated.why: Not routine in typical exertional angina; only if pulmonary embolism is suspected
No role unless the pain is epigastric and pancreatitis is suspected
Not routine in classic stable angina with a clear alternate diagnosis

decision_points: Obtain an ECG within 10 minutes of presentation and compare with prior tracings
Serial troponins are required to exclude acute coronary syndrome before labeling symptoms as stable angina
Do not order a stress test during active or unstable symptoms; risk-stratify and consider early invasive evaluation instead
Pregnancy test before stress testing or CT angiography in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Typical (classic) angina
criteria.summary: Chest discomfort that is substernal, provoked by exertion or emotional stress, and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin within minutes.
items: Substernal chest discomfort of characteristic quality and duration
Provoked by exertion or emotional stress

criteria.name: Atypical angina
criteria.summary: Chest discomfort meeting two of the three typical features.
items: Meets two of: substernal discomfort, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

criteria.name: Noncardiac chest pain
criteria.summary: Chest discomfort meeting one or none of the typical features.
items: Meets one or none of: substernal discomfort, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or myocardial infarction)
differential.why_considered: Same underlying coronary disease; the key question is whether symptoms are stable or represent an acute plaque event
differential.trigger: Pain at rest, new-onset severe pain, or a change in a previously stable pattern

history: Symptoms at rest or with minimal activity
Crescendo pattern over hours to days
Not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
labs: Elevated BNP if heart failure develops
imaging: New regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography
ST depression or elevation on ECG

differential.name: Aortic dissection
differential.why_considered: Severe chest pain that can radiate to the back and mimic cardiac ischemia
differential.trigger: Sudden severe tearing pain, pulse or blood pressure asymmetry, or a widened mediastinum

history: Abrupt onset, maximal at the start
Migrating from chest to back or abdomen
Marfan syndrome or known aortic aneurysm
labs: No single lab excludes it; troponin may be normal or mildly elevated
imaging: Intimal flap on CT angiography or transesophageal echocardiography

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Chest discomfort with shortness of breath and tachycardia
differential.trigger: Pleuritic pain, sudden dyspnea, or hypoxia with a clear chest

history: Recent surgery, immobilization, or long travel
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to findings
Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness
imaging: Filling defect on CT pulmonary angiography

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Burning chest discomfort that patients describe as indigestion

history: Burning quality, worse after meals or when lying flat

differential.name: Costochondritis
differential.why_considered: Chest wall pain that can be mistaken for cardiac pain

history: Worse with deep breath, coughing, or twisting
exam: Reproducible tenderness at the costochondral junctions

differential.name: Anxiety or panic attack
differential.why_considered: Chest tightness with palpitations, sweating, and a sense of doom

history: Occurs at rest or during stress without exertion
Associated with hyperventilation, paresthesias, or fear of dying
Episodes may last longer than typical angina

differential.name: Aortic stenosis
differential.why_considered: Exertional chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope from outflow obstruction

exam: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
labs: Elevated BNP if heart failure develops
imaging: Calcified, restricted aortic valve with elevated gradient on echocardiography

severity.mild: Stable angina with symptoms only at high levels of exertion; normal vitals and exam; normal troponin and ECG
severity.moderate: Stable angina with symptoms at moderate activity; may have risk factors and ECG changes such as LVH or prior Q waves; troponin normal
severity.severe: Unstable pattern or symptoms at rest; ECG may show ST depression or T wave inversion; troponin may be normal or slightly elevated; hemodynamics stable
severity.critical: Ongoing ischemic pain with hemodynamic instability, pulmonary edema, or malignant arrhythmia; troponin rising; requires immediate reperfusion

red_flags.finding: Pain at rest or lasting more than 20 minutes
red_flags.meaning: Unstable angina or myocardial infarction until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: New ST depression or elevation on ECG
red_flags.meaning: Acute ischemia; needs urgent risk stratification and possible reperfusion

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, or new pulmonary crackles
red_flags.meaning: Cardiogenic shock or acute heart failure from severe ischemia
Severe outflow obstruction or arrhythmia; evaluate urgently

special_populations.differences: May present with dyspnea, weakness, or confusion rather than chest pain; symptoms can be triggered by minimal activity.
Neuropathy can blunt pain, so they report breathlessness, fatigue, or indigestion instead of classic chest pressure.
Chest discomfort is more often attributed to reflux or the increased workload of pregnancy; true angina is uncommon but can occur with pre-existing coronary disease or coronary spasm.
Symptoms come on with much lighter activity, and shortness of breath may dominate over chest pressure.

key_questions.question: What does the discomfort feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Pressure, squeezing, tightness, or heaviness rather than sharp or stabbing

key_questions.question: Where do you feel it, and does it spread anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Mid-chest or substernal, radiating to the left shoulder, inner left arm, neck, jaw, or back

key_questions.question: What brings it on?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertion or emotional stress; reproducible at the same level of activity

key_questions.question: What makes it go away, and how quickly?
key_questions.looking_for: Resolves within minutes of rest or with nitroglycerin under the tongue

key_questions.question: How long does each episode last?
key_questions.looking_for: About 2 to 10 minutes; longer than 20 minutes suggests acute coronary syndrome

key_questions.question: Has the pattern changed recently — is it coming on with less activity, or at rest?
key_questions.looking_for: A crescendo pattern or rest pain means unstable angina until proven otherwise

key_questions.question: Do you get short of breath, sweat, feel nauseated, or lightheaded with the episodes?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or lightheadedness supporting myocardial ischemia

key_questions.question: Does the pain change with a deep breath, coughing, or pressing on your chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a musculoskeletal or pleural cause

key_questions.question: Does it burn after meals or when you lie down, and do antacids help?
Have you ever had a heart attack, stent, or bypass?
key_questions.looking_for: Known coronary artery disease raises the likelihood of angina

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol?
Do you smoke, or have you smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack or bypass at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Early coronary disease in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: Do you use cocaine, amphetamines, or any stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant use that can provoke coronary spasm or ischemia

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including anything for chest pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Nitroglycerin use and response, plus drugs that can trigger spasm such as triptans or ergots

key_questions.question: Any fever, coughing up blood, or recent long travel with leg swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present points toward infection, pulmonary embolism, or another cause

key_questions.question: Any sudden tearing pain that moved from your chest to your back?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for aortic dissection

reasoning_points: Substernal chest pressure provoked by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin within minutes
Episodes last about 2 to 10 minutes and are reproducible at a similar level of activity
Radiation to the left shoulder, inner left arm, neck, or jaw
Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, or nausea during episodes
Coronary risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking
ECG without acute ST elevation and serial high-sensitivity troponins that are normal or unchanged, excluding acute coronary syndrome
Alternative causes of chest pain such as aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, reflux, and chest wall pain considered and excluded
A change in pattern or rest pain would reclassify the presentation as unstable angina

easy: Middle-aged or older adult with classic exertional chest pressure relieved by rest
Clear coronary risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, and diabetes
Normal troponin and no acute ECG changes
Symptoms reproducible with the same level of activity
medium: Older adult or patient with diabetes presenting with exertional dyspnea or fatigue instead of chest pain
Atypical features such as jaw, back, or epigastric discomfort
ECG showing LVH or prior Q waves that complicate interpretation
Symptoms that overlap with reflux or musculoskeletal pain
hard: Younger patient with few traditional risk factors and atypical symptoms
Rest or nocturnal pain suggesting vasospastic angina
Chest pain in pregnancy attributed to reflux or increased cardiac workload
Presentation with nonspecific symptoms and a nondiagnostic ECG requiring stress testing or coronary imaging to confirm
